reviews.title: Great if you’re Catholic
reviews.body:
I am an Episcopal priest and have been enjoying several of the devotions on Hallow, including the Lent challenge in the Brothers Karamazov and the series in detachment, and the daily gospel.  I also have been listening to Jeff Cavins’ daily reflection and for the most part enjoy it.  

Until today. Today (6/7/2026) Jeff was dogmatic and judgmental about the Catholic understanding of the Eucharist and said that other than the Catholic point of view all others - including Episcopal, I presume - are in error.  It has become clear to me that this app’s purpose is to (a) nurture and develop the faith of Roman Catholics and (b) to convince others, including Episcopal and Orthodox Catholics (yes, Rome is not the only Catholic Church), to repent and come home to the see of Peter, which I am sure you wouldn’t hesitate to call the “one true church.” 

Jeff Cavins’ pleasant and chatty manner belies the underlying judgment he brings.  Many of his reflections are helpful and uplifting but sometimes he seems to get carried away with doctrinal arrogance.  Is Hallow at all interested in being useful and uplifting to any except Roman Catholics?

I will continue to make use of Hallow as one devotional aid among several, but sadly have been somewhat soured by its conservatism and exclusivist ecclesiology.

reviews.title: Not Affordable for People Who Really Need It
reviews.body:
I started using this app when I was admitted to hospital during a mental health crisis, and honestly, it helped me so much. It felt healing, comforting, and gave me something to hold onto when everything else was falling apart.

The problem is once I got out of hospital, my condition meant I couldn’t go back to work. That’s when I realised the price of the app is basically impossible for people who are already struggling. And I’m not the only one my own family members have told me the same thing. They loved the free trial but couldn’t keep it because of the cost-of-living crisis.

I fully respect that people who build apps deserve to be paid for their work; I’m not fighting that. But it’s still heartbreaking that something meant to bring people closer to God ends up being out of reach for the exact people who need it most.

Personally, I think it would be beautiful if the app were free, with an optional donations model or something similar. Catholics are extremely giving people, and the community would absolutely support something that helps everyone, not just those who can afford it.

I’m sharing this with love, and with the hope that the app can become more accessible to people who are going through hardship or unable to work. Spiritual tools shouldn’t be locked behind a price tag. God bless ✝️

reviews.title: The American politicisation of a Roman Catholic App
reviews.body:
I have been a very happy Hallow user from Europe, but over recent months the app has become increasingly US-focused.  And today, I am sad to say that I shall no longer be using Hallow as it has been politicised.

I had hoped that it might remain a global tool for Catholicism, but following the tragic death of Charlie Kirk, a prominent, pro-Trump, right wing political activist, both Hallow and Bishop Barron (one of its “trusted Catholic figures”), have been forthright in immediately posting prayer plans and eulogies for him.  

Any shooting is a tragedy, but this is right wing politicisation.  Nowhere is there mention of the shooting at Evergreen High School in Colorado or of the myriad of other school shootings or unnecessary deaths by gun violence that plague the US.  It should also be said that Charlie Kirk is a man who has publicly stated that an armed society and annual gun deaths are a necessary “trade-off” for liberty.  There has been nothing to pray for the families in Gaza; there has been nothing to pray for the victims of other school shootings; there has been nothing to pray for the victims of the Ukrainian invasion; there has been nothing for the migrants who die on their travels to escape torment in their home nations or who are forcibly separated from their families by government officials.

But there is immediate support for a right wing political activist.

Just to show why this is a problem, Charlie Kirkis a man who in his public debates has proposed politics that are directly contrary to the Catechism of the Catholic Church.  To provide just two as an example.  He has publicly argued for more aggressive use of the death penalty—calling for executions to be “public, quick, and televised,” specifically suggesting that children should watch as a deterrent.  According to the Catholic Catechism: “[The] Death penalty is inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person.” (CCC 2267)

He has consistently campaigned for strict immigration restriction, arguing against “welcoming foreigners” and opposing policies that allow migrants to settle in the U.S. “.  According to the Catholic Catechim:  “Prosperous nations are obliged … to welcome the foreigner.” (CCC 2241)

Not only that but he is also a proponent of Christian nationalism, advocating for blending faith and government and opposing constitutional separation of church and state.  The Church historically defends religious liberty and cautions against conflating faith with national identity in a way that undermines the dignity of all persons (see Vatican II: Dignitatis Humanae).

If your politics match with America’s right wing, then this is probably the app for you.  If your politics are from anywhere else in the world or are to the left of Donald Trump’s second term, this is not the app for you.

reviews.title:
Hallow: A Wolf in Sheep's Clothing - A Shameless Cash Grab Masquerading as a
Prayer App
reviews.body:
If you’re looking for a genuine Christian prayer app to deepen your faith, stay as far away from Hallow as possible. This app isn’t about spirituality—it’s about lining pockets under the guise of piety.

At first glance, Hallow presents itself as a serene, faith-based platform, promising guided prayers and reflections. But once you’re in, you quickly realize it’s nothing more than a paywalled cash machine, preying on sincere believers with manipulative marketing tactics. Free content is scarce, and they aggressively push expensive subscriptions, exploiting people’s devotion for profit.

Christianity teaches generosity and accessibility, yet Hallow charges absurd fees just to access basic prayer resources—things that should be freely available to anyone seeking a deeper connection with God. Their business model reeks of hypocrisy, using faith as bait while they rake in money.

The worst part? The app is riddled with invasive data tracking and relentless upselling, proving that their real mission isn’t to help people pray—it’s to exploit religious devotion for financial gain.

Save your money and your faith. There are plenty of free, honest resources out there that don’t sell prayer like a luxury product. Hallow is nothing more than a sanctimonious scam, and the fact that they do it under the banner of Christianity makes it all the more shameful.

How to get to heaven:

Turn from sin and believe

(You can look up these verses)

1- Believe that Jesus is God (John 1:1), (John 1:14) who died on the cross as a sacrifice for our sins (2 Corinth 5:18), (2 Corinth 5:21) and rose from the dead on the third day. (Acts 3:15)

2- know that you are a sinner in need of a saviour, you can’t get to heaven by trying to be a good person (Ephesians 2:8), (Romans 3:23)

3- Be sorry for your sins and be willing to stop sinning (1 Corinth 6:9-10), (Mathew 7:22)

4- Live for God and make Jesus the Lord of your life (John 3:3), (2 Corinth 5:17)

We cannot turn from sin and live for God by ourselves, we can only do it by the help of God’s Holy Spirit (that comes to live in our hearts when we do what I’ve listed here) and the Bible. God lives through us. however if we keep on resisting the Holy Spirit and hardening our hearts there is no forgiveness.
